$comment: Vendor configuration. This file is the ONLY place the monitored set is declared;
no vendor list lives in source code. Copy to vendors.json and edit, or supply your
own at deploy time.
type: which adapter parses the feed.
statuspage  Atlassian Statuspage v2 summary.json (most vendors)
instatus    Instatus summary.json (page.status UP/HASISSUES)
google      Google appsstatus incidents.json
apple       Apple system_status_en_US.js
microsoft   portal.office.com servicestatus (CONSUMER services only)
okta        Atom feed
salesforce  api.status.salesforce.com product instances
concur      open.concur.com JSON API
sorryapp    SorryApp status.json
betterstack Better Stack HTML status page
scope (optional): restrict which components count, by group or exact name.
Without it, the vendor's own page-level indicator is trusted.
With it, only the listed components decide the status.
NOT INCLUDED and why: Freshdesk, Freshservice and Paylocity publish no public
machine-readable status endpoint (verified 2026-07-30 - Freshworks' Statuspage
returns 401 'page is inactive', status.freshworks.com is a JS shell, and
status.paylocity.com redirects to their login portal). They were previously
sourced from StatusGator, a third-party aggregator, which is no longer used.
A monitored row with no real data source reports health it never verified.
status.adobe.com is a JS app; its real data lives at data.status.adobe.com
CPU, measured - against a Workers FREE-plan ceiling of 10ms for the ENTIRE
collection run across all vendors. Adobe alone would exceed the budget 7x and
kill the run for everyone else. It becomes viable on Workers Paid (30s CPU).
SOCIAL / MESSAGING - what is and is not available (probed 2026-07-31):
Discord    Statuspage, 30 components                            INCLUDED
LinkedIn   Statuspage, 11 components (www.linkedin-status.com)  INCLUDED
Slack      publishes JSON but in its own format, not Statuspage; needs a
dedicated adapter before it can be added
Meta       metastatus.com serves HTML only - no machine-readable feed
X/Twitter  api.twitterstat.us returns 401; the feed is no longer public
Signal     status.signal.org serves HTML only
Telegram   no status endpoint resolves at all
WhatsApp   no separate endpoint; Meta does not publish one
A row with no real data source reports health it never verified, so the
unavailable ones are omitted rather than faked.
FRESHWORKS (Freshdesk, Freshservice, Freshsales, Freshchat, Freshcaller) is NOT
included. Probed 2026-07-31: freshworks.statuspage.io returns 401 'page is
inactive'; status.freshworks.com and every <product>.freshstatus.io page is a
JS app whose embedded __NEXT_DATA__ holds branding only. Live status comes from
public-api.freshstatus.io/v1, which requires an account context that cannot be
inferred without executing the page's JavaScript. No combination of subdomain,
account_id or referer headers returned 200.
ADOBE - investigated twice, still excluded. status.adobe.com is a JS shell; the
real data is data.status.adobe.com/adobestatus/{SnowServiceRegistry 2.2MB,
StatusEvents 5.5MB}. JSON.parse of those measured ~70ms of CPU against a
Workers FREE-plan ceiling of 10ms for the ENTIRE run.
A lighter touch WAS attempted: regex-scanning the raw text for open products
costs 2.8ms instead of 17.4ms and matched a full parse exactly (74 hits). It was
REJECTED anyway, because the cheap signal is wrong. The marker it keys on
("endedOn":0) does not mean 'currently affecting users' - every one of those 74
products has a latest history status of 'Closed', at severity Trivial (70) or
Minor (4). Shipping it would have reported 22 Adobe products degraded while
Adobe considers them resolved: a false RED, the mirror of findings H1/H6/H7.
The authoritative signal is the newest entry of a timestamp-keyed history map
per product, which cannot be extracted without real parsing. Adobe therefore
needs Workers Paid (30s CPU per cron), not a cleverer scan.
brandDomain is DECLARED per vendor, never derived from the status URL:
www.calendlystatus.com would yield 'calendlystatus.com' and
www.cloudflarestatus.com 'cloudflarestatus.com' - neither is the brand. It is
used only by scripts/fetch-logos.mjs, which downloads each vendor's own favicon
ONCE at build time. Logos are self-hosted deliberately: hot-linking would leak
every visitor's IP to 41 companies and force widening the CSP.

vendors.$comment: health.aws.amazon.com/public/currentevents - the feed behind the AWS Health Dashboard. Served as charset=UTF-16 with a BOM, which response.text() decodes as UTF-8 per the fetch spec and turns into mojibake; collect.js decodeBody() sniffs the BOM. RESOLVED events stay in the feed, so an event counts as active only when it has no end_time AND is not marked resolved - filtering on presence alone would report AWS degraded over an incident closed hours ago. Named 'AWS' rather than 'Amazon Web Services': the dashboard filter indexes vendor and service labels, so the long name alone made the row unfindable by typing the name everyone uses. The service label carries both. Service catalogue from servicedata-us-east-1-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/services.json, found by reading the Health Dashboard's network log. currentevents lists ONLY active events, so with nothing wrong the row had no services at all. The catalogue is 5,848 service-region pairs covering 268 distinct services; snapshotted at BUILD time into config/aws-services.json (7.7 KB) by scripts/fetch-aws-catalogue.mjs. Reading it live cost a subrequest and ~1.7 ms CPU every cycle against a 10 ms ceiling production was already exceeding; the service list changes only when AWS launches a service. PINNED to shard 10: this vendor parses a large document, and hash assignment put several such vendors in one invocation, exceeding the free plan's 10 ms CPU ceiling and killing collection for 3.5 hours on 2026-08-01. Expensive vendors are kept apart deliberately.
vendors.name: AWS

AWS Private CA Connector for Active Directory

vendors.$comment: Scoped to Bubble's OWN services. Its Statuspage lists 25 components, but 18 are UPSTREAM third parties - AWS regions, Cloudflare, Intercom, SendGrid, imgix. Including them would blame Bubble for someone else's outage, and Cloudflare is already its own row here, so a Cloudflare incident would show twice and make Bubble look broken. Same principle as the Cloudflare scoping decision: report what the vendor says about ITS OWN service.
vendors.name: Bubble

vendors.$comment: Cloudflare publishes ~470 components, most of them edge PoPs. Routine re-routing in far-flung data centres is the redundancy WORKING, not an outage, so scope to the services group. Measured 2026-07-30: unscoped = 46 non-operational (false red); services only = 0.
vendors.name: Cloudflare

vendors.$comment: status_history, NOT the incidents feed. That feed is 23.3 MB - the complete incident history back to 2013 - re-downloaded and re-parsed every cycle to find the few that are open, and no filter exists (open, status, limit and days all return the identical 23,354,922 bytes). Parsing it measured 69 ms CPU against a 10 ms ceiling and was the largest single contributor to the 2026-08-01 outage. status_history is keyed by SERVICE with a Current Status for each, at 35-300 KB per data centre. All four are read and merged worst-wins: reading only us2 would report Concur healthy while EU customers were down. PINNED to shard 2.
vendors.name: Concur

vendors.$comment: Services live at GROUP level; leaves are per-datacentre instances. MIGRATION WATCH: Docusign is moving to health.docusign.com (a Next.js app whose embedded state carries only locale strings - status is fetched client-side, so it is not parseable yet). status.docusign.com still returns 200 as of 2026-07-31. When the old endpoint is retired this row fails closed to unknown with a visible warning - it cannot rot to green the way findings H6 and H7 did - so switch it when health.docusign.com exposes a machine-readable feed.
vendors.name: Docusign

vendors.$comment: Google publishes its product catalogue separately from its incidents feed; componentsUrl supplies the list so every product can be shown, with open incidents marked.
vendors.name: Google

vendors.$comment: cloud.ibm.com/status/getEnhancedStatus - found only by loading the page in a real browser and reading the network log; the URL is built at runtime so no static string in the 3.4 MB bundle matches it. Parsed by TARGETED SCAN, not JSON.parse: the payload is 2.44 MB and measured 8.03 ms CPU to parse whole versus 1.82 ms to indexOf-scan, against a 10 ms free-plan budget for the ENTIRE run. Only 26 of 1,293 items are incidents; the rest are release notes and announcements. No query parameter filters it - state, days, limit and type were all tried and all return the identical 2,556,694 bytes. PINNED to shard 11: this vendor parses a large document, and hash assignment put several such vendors in one invocation, exceeding the free plan's 10 ms CPU ceiling and killing collection for 3.5 hours on 2026-08-01. Expensive vendors are kept apart deliberately.
vendors.name: IBM Cloud
Iorad
vendors.$comment: SorryApp splits components onto a second endpoint, advertised in the page payload itself as links.components.href with count 10. Without it the row showed a page-level status and nothing underneath. Names repeat (two 'iorad editor', two 'iorad player') because SorryApp lists them per environment; the adapter dedupes by name keeping the worst.
Services live at GROUP level here; the leaf components are per-data-centre instances. Listing leaves would show infrastructure, not services.

vendors.$comment: metastatus.com is a JS app; data lives at /data/orgs.json, found in its bundle. Covers BUSINESS/DEVELOPER platforms only - Graph API, Marketing API, WhatsApp Business Platform - NOT consumer Facebook, Instagram or WhatsApp. PINNED to shard 6 to balance the cycle: hashing left shard 6 empty while shard 8 carried six vendors, wasting a whole minute of the 15-minute cycle.

vendors.$comment: ONE row for Microsoft, merged from every public feed they publish. As five sibling rows these sorted apart alphabetically and read as five unrelated companies. Row severity is the WORST across sources, and a source that fails contributes an `unknown` component rather than being dropped - otherwise the row could read green while a fifth of it was never checked. GitHub and LinkedIn are Microsoft-owned but stay separate: readers think of them as their own brands, and folding them in would hide a GitHub outage under a Microsoft row. Complete map of what Microsoft publishes: /api/posts/{id} accepts exactly four ids (azure, m365Consumer, mac, ppac), brute-forced across 40+ product names; Azure DevOps is on its own host. Enterprise per-workload health (Exchange, SharePoint, Entra, Intune, Defender) is tenant-scoped behind the authenticated Graph Service Health API and is not public.
vendors.name: Microsoft

vendors.$comment: Okta runs on Salesforce Experience Cloud with no public JSON API (summary.json, index.json, history.atom and history.rss all 401). The page embeds its incidents as JSON and the adapter parses that. The previous FeedBurner Atom source returned 200 but its newest entry was 456 days old - a feed that reports healthy forever is the same silent rot as findings H6 and H7.
vendors.name: Okta

vendors.$comment: components_v2.json, NOT status.json. status.json is 173 B and Statuspage-shaped so it needed no code, but it carries only a page-level indicator and produced a row with ZERO components - technically correct and useless, since a reader cannot see which Oracle service is affected. components_v2.json is 1.63 MB and measured 3.17 ms to JSON.parse, affordable against the 10 ms budget (unlike IBM's 2.44 MB, which needed a targeted scan - measure, do not assume). It holds 8,730 region-service pairs; the adapter rolls them into 119 SERVICES, each carrying the worst status across regions, with affected regions in the description rather than the name. brandDomain is the STATUS host, not oracle.com: oracle.com answers 403 to our honest User-Agent, and forging a browser UA to scrape a logo would contradict audit finding L2. The status host serves the same Oracle mark and does not block us. PINNED to shard 14: this vendor parses a large document, and hash assignment put several such vendors in one invocation, exceeding the free plan's 10 ms CPU ceiling and killing collection for 3.5 hours on 2026-08-01. Expensive vendors are kept apart deliberately.
vendors.name: Oracle Cloud

vendors.$comment: componentLevel 'group' because the leaves are REGIONS. scope picks the US leaves that VOTE on severity (US-focus decision 2026-08-03); the groups still display, carrying non-US trouble as card detail that informs without voting.
vendors.name: OutSystems

vendors.$comment: Instatus splits page state and components across two endpoints; summary.json carries only page.status. componentsUrl is advisory - if it fails the page status still decides severity. PINNED to shard 7 so IBM Cloud and Oracle Cloud, the two largest parses left, each get an invocation to themselves.
vendors.name: Perplexity

vendors.$comment: Services live at GROUP level here; the leaf components are per-data-centre instances. Listing leaves would show infrastructure, not services. PINNED to shard 4 so IBM Cloud and Oracle Cloud, the two largest parses left, each get an invocation to themselves.
vendors.name: QuantumWorkplace

vendors.$comment: CORRECTION: an earlier note claimed Seismic 'publishes 54 region names and no groups', and componentLevel 'none' suppressed the whole list on that basis. That was wrong. Only the first 20 components are data centres (U.S. East3, CAN1 (Canada), DE1 (Germany)...); the remaining 34 are real SERVICES - Aura Copilot, Digital Sales Room, DocCenter, LiveSend, Seismic Content API, Writebacks and the rest. Scoped to the services by name; the data centres are excluded because points of presence are not what a reader is asking about. The scope mechanism warns when a configured name matches nothing, so a Seismic rename surfaces as drift rather than a silently shrinking list.
vendors.name: Seismic
